title: Trump Turned a Refugee Bureau Into a $410 Million Deportation Machine
excerpt: A Washington Post investigation reveals the State Department's new "Office of Remigration" has committed at least $410 million to secret deals with 31 countries to accept deportees who aren't their citizens.
body:
• A Washington Post investigation published September 21, 2026, found the Trump administration repurposed a State Department bureau that once handled refugee affairs into the "Office of Remigration," created in May 2025.
  • The administration authorized or pledged at least $410 million for agreements with 31 countries through the end of June: $81 million earmarked for governments that signed deals, over $178 million for the International Organization for Migration (IOM), and over $123 million for the UN refugee agency UNHCR.
  • Forbidden Stories counted at least 25,447 people deported to third countries between January 2025 and August 31, 2026; agreements were reached with at least 35 countries, roughly 20,000 deportees sent to Mexico and the rest to 27 other countries across Latin America, Africa and the Pacific.
  • US law bars deporting people to countries where they may face persecution; DHS instead routes them to third countries, where lawyers say deportees are held without charge in what amounts to a "legal black hole."

A refugee bureau, repurposed

Inside the State Department, the bureau that once handled refugee affairs now has a different mission. According to internal government records obtained by The Washington Post, the Trump administration transformed that office into the "Office of Remigration" in May 2025 tasking it with negotiating secret deportation agreements with foreign governments. The investigation, published September 21, 2026, was produced with a Forbidden Stories consortium of roughly 24 media organizations, including The Guardian.

The office is headed by Christian Jove Ehrhardt, 41, a career diplomat who spent nearly two decades in the department's security branch before being summoned to Washington last year to lead the new operation. His assignment: persuade countries — mostly in Africa and Latin America — to accept flights of migrants deported from the United States who are not their citizens.

The money trail

The Post reports that at least $410 million was authorized or pledged to facilitate the agreements with 31 countries, tallied through the end of June. Of that, $81 million was earmarked directly for governments that signed deals. Over $178 million went to the International Organization for Migration and more than $123 million to UNHCR — institutions built to protect the displaced, now receiving American funds to help move deportees through the third-country pipeline.

Forbidden Stories found the US deported at least 25,447 people to third countries between January 2025 and August 31, 2026. Agreements were reached with at least 35 countries — 28 have already received deportees, seven more are expected to. About 20,000 went to Mexico; the rest were flown to 27 other countries across Latin America, Africa and the Pacific. Of Africa's 54 countries, 49 were approached.

Ehrhardt himself toured West Africa in mid-June — Ivory Coast, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Togo and Gabon — stops that preceded new agreements in the region.

Legal gray zones and leverage

US law prohibits deporting people to countries where they may face persecution. Instead of testing that bar, the Department of Homeland Security routes deportees to third countries — places they may never have set foot in. Lawyers interviewed for the investigation describe deportees held without charge in those destinations as thrown into a "legal black hole," with no clear jurisdiction to hear their claims and no timeline for release.

"Deportees held without charge in third countries are thrown into a legal black hole."

— Immigration lawyers interviewed by The Washington Post

The deals are not all persuasion by checkbook. A separate AFP investigation found that US visa bans and travel restrictions were used as leverage to pressure African governments into signing. The effort is spearheaded at the White House by deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration's immigration agenda, according to the Post.

The diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora, the reporting lands on both sides of the ledger. Asylum and refugee pathways that some Indian nationals rely on are shrinking at the same time the deportation apparatus is growing. An Indian national who loses an immigration case no longer faces only removal to India; under the third-country framework, they could be sent to a country in Africa or Latin America with no connection to them, where legal options are thinner. India has negotiated its own readmission terms with Washington, but these deals mean the final destination is no longer guaranteed to be the deportee's home country.

What's next

The third-country program already faces legal challenges, with courts weighing whether routing deportees through intermediary nations circumvents statutory protections against refoulement. With seven more countries expected to begin receiving flights and hundreds of millions committed through UN agencies, the Office of Remigration appears set to become a permanent fixture of US immigration enforcement. For diaspora communities, immigration attorneys' advice is unchanged but more urgent: anyone in proceedings should know exactly where a removal order could send them, because the answer may no longer be "home."
image_caption: US President Donald Trump turned a refugee bureau into a $410 million deportation machine.
nri_angle: With refugee and asylum pathways shrinking while the deportation apparatus grows, Indian nationals caught in US immigration limbo face a new risk: removal not to India, but to a third country they may never have visited, where their legal options are thinner.
